Thank you, Mr. Chair. Israel acknowledges the opportunity to continue to engage in an open discussion on the scope of the application of universal jurisdiction within the framework of the Sixth Committee. At the outset, Israel recognizes the efforts undertaken by the Sixth Committee, the Working Group and the Secretary-General to allow Member States to better understand the scope of the principle of universal jurisdiction under domestic and international law, as well as the full range of diverging views of States on this topic. Israel shares the view regarding the importance of combating impunity and ensuring that the perpetrators of the most serious crimes are brought to justice. In line with this longstanding principle position, Israel also shares concerns expressed by many states regarding the potential of abuse or misuse of universal jurisdiction, including its exercise in politically motivated, selective or discriminatory manner. All too often, different actors have taken advantage of domestic legislation attempting to advance political agendas by filing spurious complaints with unsubstantiated allegations of serious crimes. Indeed, the pursuit of such complaints may not only undermine the principles of sovereignty, subsidiarity, and international committee, but also erode the legitimacy and credibility of international law, adversely impact diplomatic relation, and undermine international cooperation. Therefore, it is crucial that the exercise of universal jurisdiction be strictly reserved as a mechanism of last resort and that strong measures are incorporated into domestic legislation to safeguard against misuse and politicization. Such safeguards may include that any decision regarding the exercise of universal jurisdiction be made at the preliminary stages of proceeding by the highest ranking officials of the executive of the forum state. after consulting the state with the closest jurisdictional links and only subject to explicit written waiver of immunity by it. In this context, it is critical to recall the customary obligation to respect ratione personae and ratione materiae immunities of any state officials acting in their official capacity on behalf of the state. Improper exercise of universal jurisdiction carries with it the risk of violating the principle of immunity under international customary law, as well as the sovereign equality of states and threaten the conduct of international relations and the stability of global affairs. Mr. Chair, as noted by Israel previously and as remain evident by the recent Secretary General's report, there continue to be divergent views within the international community on key issues regarding the scope of universal jurisdiction, such as its definition, legal status, and conditions for applications. The identification of sufficient relevant state practice on the assertion of universal jurisdiction continues to present a significant methodological challenge. Particularly, lack of publicly available data regarding state practice results in a misleading and distorted picture in this regard. Especially, the range of legal grounds on which national prosecutor decided to refrain from initiating, admitting or prosecuting a complaint under the principle of universal jurisdiction generally remain publicly unavailable. Indeed, it is seldom made part of the public record whether a complaint is unfounded, unlikely to succeed on merits, or the subject of complaint enjoys immunity under customary international law. Significant differences reflected in the scarce state practice and opinio juris and lack of available material data regarding state practice clearly highlights that it is both premature and inappropriate as a matter of law to consider rules and standards for universal jurisdiction. Moreover, treaty obligation to extradite or prosecute are not in and of themselves to be understood as reflecting universal jurisdiction, nor should they be referenced as an evidence reflecting state practice in this regard. These two concepts are and should remain legally distinct. Mr. Chair, in order to prevent abuse, it is essential that the principle of universal jurisdiction remains a mechanism of last resort applied in accordance with other principles of international law, such as the principles of sovereign equality of states, subsidiarity and territorial integrity, as well as immunity under international customary law. Given the lack of state practice and divergence of views, further study of state practice is indeed necessary and critical to understanding whether and how further rules could or should be implemented. Accordingly, the utmost restraint is and should be exercised before resorting to universal jurisdiction. This restraint must be exercised until such time that we internationally agree upon safeguards to guide the application of universal jurisdiction, including criteria for impartiality and non-politicization. These safeguards must have regard for state sovereignty, immunities and due process. I thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank you for your statement and I now invite the representative of the Kingdom of the Netherlands to deliver his statement. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. The Kingdom of the Netherlands aligns itself with the statement given by the European Union on behalf of the EU and its member states. In addition to this statement, the Kingdom of the Netherlands would like to share the following. In the view of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, universal jurisdiction is an important tool in the fight against impunity for the most serious crimes under international law. Furthermore, universal jurisdiction contributes to implementing the principle of complementarity under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court. This topic has been discussed in the Sixth Committee for some years now, and even though some progress has been achieved, it is also clear that the views and practices of States concerning the scope and application of the principle of universal jurisdiction vary widely. For the Netherlands, The most relevant piece of legislation concerning universal jurisdiction is the International Crimes Act of June 19, 2003, which entered into force in October 2003. Article 2 of the International Crimes Act states that, without prejudice to the relevant provisions of the Criminal Code and the Code of Military Law, Dutch criminal law shall apply to: a) anyone who commits any of the crimes defined in this Act outside the Netherlands if the suspect is present in the Netherlands; b) anyone who commits any of the crimes defined in this Act outside the Nederlands if the crime is committed against a Dutch national; c) a Dutch national who commits any of the crimes defined in this Act outside the Netherlands. In terms of providing a basis for the exercise of universal jurisdiction by the Netherlands, the first element mentioned above is the most relevant part, as it allows the authorities to investigate and prosecute the crimes covered by the International Crimes Act when these have been committed abroad by foreign nationals. However, the International Crimes Act does not provide for full, unlimited jurisdiction in respect of international crimes. The judicial authorities of the Netherlands cannot open an investigation into alleged international crimes committed abroad by foreigners against non-nationals without the suspect having been identified and present in the country. Investigations into a general situation are not possible unless the victim and/or the alleged perpetrator is a Dutch national, according to Article 2. In other cases, Dutch authorities are therefore only competent to investigate universal jurisdiction cases if the suspect is present on the territory during investigation. In such cases, the decision to investigate and prosecute is based on a decision by the public prosecutor's office. In addition to the International Crimes Act, the Netherlands Criminal Code, to be precise, Article 381, provides a basis for the exercise of universal jurisdiction by the Netherlands over the crime of piracy committed on the high seas. Under Dutch law, dual criminality is not a prerequisite for the investigation and prosecution of international crimes. The Kingdom of the Netherlands support the ILC study and awaits its result. I thank you, Mr. Chair.

Its application shall be consistent with international law and the conduct of international relations. Chair, Egypt aligns with the statements delivered on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement, the African Group and by Brazil on behalf of a group of states and would like to add four brief points in its national capacity. First, Egypt reaffirms its commitment to the fight against impunity, especially for offenses that amount to international crimes. Second, Egypt underscores the primacy of the principle of territoriality. Universal jurisdiction remains a subsidiary and residual means for holding alleged offenders charged with the perpetration of international crimes if the territorial state or other relevant forum states such as those exercising active person jurisdiction are unable or unwilling to exercise jurisdiction. In this regard, Egypt recalls the view expressed by President Gilbert Guillaume in a separate opinion appended to the ICJ judgment in the arrest warrant case of 2002, quote, The adoption of the UN Charter proclaiming the sovereign equality of states and the appearance on the international scene of new states born of decolonization have strengthened the territorial principle. International criminal law has itself undergone considerable development and constitutes today an impressive legal corpus. It recognizes in many situations the possibility or even the obligation of a state other than that on whose territory the offense was committed to confer jurisdiction on its courts to prosecute the authors of certain crimes where they are present on its territory. International criminal courts have also been created, but at no time has it been envisaged that jurisdiction should be conferred upon the courts of every state in the world to prosecute such crimes whoever their authors and victims, and irrespective of the place where the offender is to be found. To do this would, however, risk creating total judicial chaos." End quote. Third, Egypt reaffirms that when considering the question of universal jurisdiction, it is imperative to operate on the basis of a proper definition of this concept. In our view, a distinguishing feature of universal jurisdiction is that it entails the competence of a state to prosecute alleged offenders where other jurisdictional bases, including territorial, active or passive nationality, are unavailable. In other words, a hallmark of universal jurisdiction is the absence of any link between the crime and the prescribing state. Fourth, universal jurisdiction must not be conflated with other concepts such as out there out to the car. The existence of an obligation to prosecute or extradite in certain treaty regimes is not supportive of claims supporting the emergence of a rule of universal jurisdiction in relation to international crimes. Indeed, in a joint separate opinion by judges Higgins, Kooiman's and Bergenthal, also in the arrest warrant case of 2002, stated the following in relation to treaty regimes that established non-territorial bases for the exercise of jurisdiction, quote, these may properly be described as treaty based broad extraterritorial jurisdiction. In addition to these were the parallel provisions whereby a state party in whose jurisdiction the alleged perpetrator of such offenses is found shall prosecute him or extradite him. By the loose use of language, the latter has come to be referred to universal jurisdiction, though this is really an obligatory territorial jurisdiction over persons albeit in relation to acts committed elsewhere." In short, and in conclusion, Egypt is of the view that treaty regimes establishing non-territorial forms of jurisdiction are not probative for the purpose of establishing a permissive rule of universal jurisdiction in international law. Thank you.

A state invoking universal jurisdiction claims to exercise jurisdiction over any offender irrespective of his or her nationality, place of commission of offence or any link between the state and the offender. Crimes prosecuted under universal jurisdiction are considered crimes against all, too serious to tolerate jurisdictional arbitrage. It allows a state to investigate and prosecute a national of any state within their borders who is alleged to have committed certain serious crimes. The principle of universal jurisdiction in relation to piracy was codified in the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, 1982. Mr. Chair. Thank you, Mr. Chair. The Philippines thanks the Secretary General for his report and we welcome this opportunity to contribute to the committee's consideration of this agenda item by setting out Philippine state practice on the scope and application of the principle of universal jurisdiction. In Philippine law, general rule remains to be that of territoriality. and the exercise of universal jurisdiction is exceptional and reserved to the most serious offenses, which are customarily subjects of universal condemnation by the international community. Principle of universal jurisdiction is therefore recognized, but to a limited extent within the parameters defined by statute and case law. The earliest articulation of the principle of universal jurisdiction appears in a case decided by the Supreme Court in 1922, where the court affirmed jurisdiction over acts of piracy committed on the high seas. There, the court held that piracy is an offense against all humankind, hostis humani generis, which any state may punish regardless of the offender's or the victim's nationality. It stands as the earliest Philippine example of the domestic application of universal jurisdiction through municipal law. A more contemporary expression is found in statute, that is Republic Act number 9851, the Philippine law on crimes against international humanitarian law, genocide, and other crimes against humanity. Section 17 of this law provides that the state shall exercise jurisdiction regardless of where the crime is committed if, one, the accused is a Filipino citizen, two, the accused, regardless of nationality, is present in the Philippines, or three, the accused has committed the crime against a Filipino citizen. This departs from the pure, quote unquote, universal jurisdiction as in the case of piracy. Instead, it requires certain links or nexus for jurisdiction to arise. This law also allows the Philippines to prosecute alleged offenders found in its territory for certain crimes under the principle of. In this regard, the law does not make prosecution contingent on the impossibility of extradition. The law provides that in the interest of justice, Philippine authorities may defer investigation or prosecution if another state or international tribunal is already undertaking proceedings and may surrender or extradite the accused pursuant to applicable laws and treaties. However, this is discretionary in nature. So the Philippines may retain competence to prosecute even when extradition is possible. And this reflects a complimentary, not residual form of jurisdiction intended to prevent impunity while respecting the role of other competent jurisdictions. The same provision integrates safeguards against duplicative proceedings, including deference to ongoing cases and the application of ne bis in idem, precluding prosecution where a person has been finally tried abroad. These mechanisms ensure that Philippine jurisdiction operates in a cooperative and non-duplicative manner, consistent with international comity, the orderly administration of justice, and the objective of addressing impunity. Accordingly, Philippine law reflects two distinct approaches or perspectives to universal jurisdiction. One is the pure form, rooted in the law of piracy as a crime under customary international law, and the so-called subsidiary form, which is what we find in statute. In this case, it is not independent of link or nexus, but it makes jurisdiction contingent on at least one of the three statutory bases for jurisdiction. Mr. Chair, as the committee moves towards establishing the working group at its 81st session, the Philippines underscores the importance of conceptual precision in this regard. Universal jurisdiction must be clearly distinguished from other forms of extraterritorial jurisdiction and from the competence of international criminal tribunals. Ambiguity in this regard risks undermining predictability and coherence in the application of international criminal law. Philippines further recalls that the legitimacy of universal jurisdiction rests upon its disciplined use. It must be exercised in strict conformity with international law and in a manner consistent with the principles of sovereign equality, the immunities of state officials, and it must be taken to reinforce and not disrupt the international legal order grounded in the rule of law and sovereign equality. Mr. Vice Chair, Singapore thanks the Secretary-General for his report on this agenda item. We also express our appreciation to Member States for submitting information and observations. The principle of universal jurisdiction is an important weapon in the international community's arsenal for the fight against impunity, as it allows perpetrators to be held responsible for the crimes they have committed. My delegation would like to reiterate four key points on the principle of universal jurisdiction, which we think should be borne in mind. First, universal jurisdiction is not and should not be the primary basis for the exercise of criminal jurisdiction by states. Instead, the primary basis should be the territoriality principle or the nationality principle. This means that the main responsibility for the exercise of criminal jurisdiction lies with the state in whose territory the crime has occurred or the state of nationality of the alleged perpetrator. Universal jurisdiction should only be invoked as a last resort to prevent the alleged perpetrator from continuing to act with impunity in situations where no state is able or willing to exercise the other established bases of jurisdiction, including the territoriality and nationality principles. This serves to reduce the potential for abuse while ensuring that the perpetrators of the most heinous crimes are held accountable. Second, the principle of universal jurisdiction should only be applied in respect of particularly grave crimes which are of interest to or affect the international community as a whole and where there is general agreement by the international community that it would be appropriate to apply the principle. In this respect, we note that there remains significant variance as to the specific crimes which delegations consider to be crimes of international concern subject to universal jurisdiction. Third, we should keep in mind a clear distinction between, on the one hand, the exercise of universal jurisdiction, which is a principle of customary international law, And on the other hand, the exercise of jurisdiction pursuant to a treaty obligation to extradite or prosecute, or the exercise of jurisdiction by international tribunals constituted under specific treaty regimes. The exercise of jurisdiction in each of these scenarios has different sets of considerations, juridical basis, objectives, and rationales. They should not be conflated. Finally, universal jurisdiction exists within the larger international legal order. It cannot be applied in isolation from or to the exclusion of other applicable principles of international law. These principles include the immunity of state officials from foreign criminal jurisdiction, state sovereignty and territorial integrity. Universal jurisdiction must also be applied in a manner consistent with the principles of due process, transparency, rules of procedure and evidence, and international comity, amongst others. Thus, The subsidiary application of the principle of universal jurisdiction by States remains an absolute necessity to effectively fight impunity, given the commission of crimes which are not subject to the statute of limitations. So the Republic of Guinea has transposed into its domestic legislation provisions pertaining to the implementation of the Rome Treaty establishing the International Criminal Court through its laws 59 and 60 of the 26th of October 2016 on the Criminal Code and the Criminal Procedural Code respectively. Henceforth, it is in favour of prosecuting those who have ordered, perpetrated and are complicit in such crimes not subject to the statute of limitations. My delegation also commits to the application of the principle of universal jurisdiction with criteria based on nationality and territoriality. The Republic of Guinea furthermore support the prosecution or extradition of the perpetrators of such crimes pursuant to aut dedere aut judicare, the obligation to extradite or to try. In order to achieve this, the principle of universal jurisdiction must be utilised whilst respecting the primacy granted to the subsidiarity principle. My delegation welcomes the idea of the establishment of a working group during the 81st regular session of the work of the UN General Assembly, in line with resolution 79/127, to examine the question of the principle of universal jurisdiction or whether it is distinct from other similar notions. Madam President, my delegation would like to begin by expressing its thanks to the Secretary General for report A/AT/274, which provides full and detailed information on the situation of human rights in Argentina. and valuable information about the views of States on the principle of universal jurisdiction. The most serious crimes for the international community as a whole must not go unpunished. It is the duty of States to exercise their criminal jurisdiction against the perpetrators of these crimes. primary responsibility to carry out such investigations and prosecutions falls to the state on whose territory the crime was committed or to the states that have some connection to such crime, be it through the nationality of the perpetrator or the victims. However, in some circumstances when states with the primary responsibility are either unable or unwilling to exercise jurisdiction, other states that do not have a direct link to the crime can fill this void on the basis of the exercise of universal jurisdiction to prevent impunity. This is, however, a tool of an exceptional nature and that should be applied in a subsidiary manner regulated by treaty norms and customary law which should be used in line with the law. In this context Argentina understands that there should be clear rules governing the exercise of universal jurisdiction. Indeed unlimited universal jurisdiction could generate conflicts of jurisdiction between states, subjecting individuals to potential procedural abuses or even give rise to politically motivated judicial persecution. Argentine justice has on several occasions exercised universal jurisdiction through on the basis of the serious nature of crimes, particularly in relation to genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and grave violations of human rights. In Argentine judicial practice, universal jurisdiction is applied in a subsidiary and exceptional manner to the principle of territoriality and personality. This following a consideration that the crimes were either not tried or could not be tried by the states on whose territories the crimes were committed or by the states of nationality of the perpetrator or the victims. Chairman, while there is not a specific rule that regulates this jurisdiction in our domestic law, jurisprudential practice in Argentina indicates that national courts have admitted the application of this principle on the basis of our national constitution. Indeed, Article 118 of our Constitution allows the initiation of prosecutions for crimes against international law. Article 75 incorporates into our national legal order various human rights treaties which in some cases specifically allow for the application of universal jurisdiction and in other cases provide for the extraterritorial application of Argentine criminal law through the criteria of jurisdiction on the basis of active or passive nationality of those involved or the presence of the alleged perpetrator on national territory. In turn, law that implements the Rome Statute expressly grants Argentine federal courts jurisdiction over international crimes that are mentioned in the Rome Statute. Also, as a practice, before applying universal jurisdiction, Argentine judicial authorities must first ensure that there are no ongoing investigations in the country or countries involved and that the International Criminal Court is not investigating the facts. To conclude, Argentina reiterates its readiness to continue considering this matter within the Sixth Committee and to make the necessary efforts to ensure that we make specific, concrete headway. Thank you.
